By [Melinda Yao](https://www.nbcnews.com/author/melinda-yao-ncpn1312747) and [Joe Murphy](https://www.nbcnews.com/author/joe-murphy-ncpn920391)

Measles, one of the most contagious viruses in the world, is regularly infecting people in the U.S. again.

Already in 2026 more than 2,000 cases have been counted, making 2026 one of the two worst years for measles infections in the U.S. since 2000.

NBC News is continuing to track confirmed measles cases across the United States, using Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data.

Measles case counts reached a 34-year high last year, and a surge in weekly counts shows the virus is continuing to spread this year. In the second full week of the new year 296 new cases were reported. Since then case counts have been lower.

The disease epicenter at the start of the year was in South Carolina, where the CDC has confirmed 600-plus measles cases. As of late January, [more than 500 people were in quarantine and hundreds infected in the state](https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/south-carolina-measles-outbreak-surpasses-texas-vaccines-rcna256030). [State officials declared the South Carolina outbreak over](https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/south-carolina-measles-outbreak-over-nearly-1000-cases-rcna342358) in April.

The map below will be updated regularly to show year-to-date new measles case counts reported in each state and Washington, D.C.

Measles infection counts skyrocketed last year with 2,288 confirmed cases, the most reported since 1991. This comes despite the virus being marked as being “eliminated” in the U.S. —a designation meaning it is no longer constantly circulating — in 2000. [The U.S. is in danger of losing that status following a year of continuous spread of the disease](https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/measles-spread-year-elimination-status-rcna255008).

[Three people, including two young girls, died in the U.S.](https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/measles-south-carolina-quarantine-utah-arizona-us-rcna248435) from measles last year.

The major outbreaks last year began with [West Texas](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/measles-outbreak-mennonites-west-texas-seminole-vaccines-rcna208284) in February. In October, a measles outbreak occurred along the [Utah and Arizona border](https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/measles-spreading-utah-arizona-outbreak-vaccines-rcna238757). In all, the CDC recorded 49 measles outbreaks in 2025, up from 16 in 2024. So far in 2026, 30 measles outbreaks have been reported.

[Childhood vaccination rates have been backsliding](https://www.nbcnews.com/specials/vaccine-divide/index.html), leaving communities vulnerable to this deadly disease.

The measles vaccine was introduced in 1963, marking a turning point for the contagious disease, which used to infect hundreds of thousands and kill thousands in the country every year.

**CORRECTION (Feb. 20, 2026, 3:57 p.m. ET):** A previous version of a graphic in this article miscalculated the relative size of this year's measles case count. As of Feb. 20, this year's case count is four times the size of 2025's at the same point in the year, and 25 times the size of 2024's at the same point, not seven times and 30 times higher.

# Situation Report #4: Measles in the Americas Region. 4 June 2026

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| [Download](/sites/default/files/2026/06/paho-measles-sitrep4.pdf "Situation Report #4: Measles in the Americas Region. 4 June 2026") | Between epidemiological week (EW) 1 and EW 21 of 2026 (ending on 30 May 2026), the Region of the Americas reported **21,431** confirmed measles cases from 17 countries and territories, including **31** deaths, representing a 234% increase compared to the same period in 2025. Mexico (11,184), Guatemala (6,655), the United States (1,983) and Canada (1,042) accounted for the majority (97%) of confirmed cases.  During EW 19 and EW 20 of 2026, the Region of the Americas reported **1,040** new confirmed measles cases across nine countries and territories, representing a 16.2% decrease compared with the previous two-week period (EW17-18; 1,343 new cases). This decline was driven primarily by sustained reductions in the United Stated and continued decreases in Canada and Mexico. Peru was the main exception, with cases continuing to increase during this period, mostly concentrated in Puno. Trends in Guatemala should be interpreted with caution, given possible reporting delays or updates in recent weeks2.  The outbreak continues to disproportionately affect young children, with the highest incidence rates observed among infants under one year of age. Approximately 85% of confirmed cases are either unvaccinated or have an unknown vaccination status. The D8 genotype, DSId 9171 has been identified across multiple countries and remains the main genotype detected in the Region.  Model-based estimates of transmission as of EW 21 indicate continued declines in Mexico and Canada, sustained increases in Peru, and stabilizing dynamics in the United States, with the effective reproduction number (Rₜ) near 1. Full estimates and four-week forecasts are presented in **Table 3**. Nevertheless, sustained transmission could still occur through gradual, drop-by-drop spread, underscoring the need to continue strengthening vaccination efforts. |

This mismatch between the assigned source_type and the actual nature of a PMC-hosted article is a meaningful metadata inconsistency that warrants attention. source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify CDC official surveillance pages, MMWR reports, and CDC measles case count tables reporting confirmed, probable, or suspected Measles cases and deaths in the United States during 2025-01-01 to 2025-03-31.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: CDC is the primary national public health authority for Measles surveillance in the US. Their MMWR weekly reports, measles case count pages, and outbreak investigation reports are the highest-priority extractable collection sources.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify state and local health department outbreak alerts, press releases, and situation reports for Measles cases in US states and territories during Q1 2025.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: State health departments (e.g., Texas DSHS, New York DOH, California CDPH) issue outbreak alerts and case counts that may predate or supplement CDC national aggregates, providing subnational_location and locality granularity.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify NNDSS (National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System) data tables or exports for Measles (Rubeola) in the United States for weeks covering 2025-01-01 to 2025-03-31.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: NNDSS is the authoritative structured surveillance dataset for nationally notifiable diseases including Measles in the US, providing weekly case counts by jurisdiction.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify WHO and PAHO situation reports or disease surveillance bulletins that include Measles case counts for the United States or the Americas region covering Q1 2025.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: WHO and PAHO independently aggregate Measles data from member states including the US, providing an independent validation source against CDC-reported figures.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify structured open-data sources (e.g., HealthData.gov, CDC open data portal, Our World in Data) with Measles case or death counts for the United States in 2025.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: Structured databases provide machine-readable counts that can be compared against extracted records from official narrative sources for cross-validation.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify CDC case definitions, CSTE position statements, and clinical guidance documents for Measles (Rubeola) applicable to 2025 US surveillance.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: Case definitions determine whether counts are confirmed, probable, or suspected. Understanding the operative case definition is essential for correct field mapping and count semantics.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify peer-reviewed literature or preprints describing Measles epidemiology, outbreak investigations, or surveillance findings in the United States in 2025.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: Published outbreak investigations may contain granular case counts, hospitalization rates, and demographic breakdowns not available in surveillance summaries.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify reputable news reports (Reuters, AP, NPR, ProMED) covering Measles outbreaks or case counts in the United States during January–March 2025.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: News reports may surface early outbreak signals, state-level case counts, or death reports that precede official agency publication, and can guide targeted official source retrieval.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Flag any sources that report Measles-like illness without laboratory confirmation, mix Measles with Rubella or Roseola counts, or report vaccine adverse events only (VAERS) without confirmed case data.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: Sources conflating excluded disease terms (rubella, roseola, German measles, varicella) or reporting only VAERS events without case confirmation must be quarantined and reviewed before extraction.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Flag sources with ambiguous count semantics (cumulative vs. newly reported, annual vs. Q1-only) or reporting periods substantially broader than 2025-01-01 to 2025-03-31 for human review.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: Cumulative annual counts or multi-year aggregates may not be attributable to the Q1 2025 task window without additional decomposition, requiring human judgment.

planned_source_categories.why_relevant: CDC is the primary US national public health authority. CDC measles case count pages (cdc.gov/measles), MMWR weekly/early release reports, and outbreak investigation reports are the highest-priority extractable sources for confirmed, probable, and suspected Measles cases and deaths in the US during Q1 2025.

State health departments (Texas DSHS, New York DOH, California CDPH, Florida DOH, etc.) and county/local health departments issue outbreak alerts, press releases, and situation reports with subnational and locality-level Measles case counts that may predate CDC national aggregates.

NNDSS (National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System) provides weekly Measles case counts by US jurisdiction. CDC publishes NNDSS tables at wonder.cdc.gov and in MMWR. This is the authoritative structured surveillance dataset for nationally notifiable diseases including Measles.

WHO and PAHO independently aggregate Measles surveillance data from member states including the US. WHO measles surveillance data, PAHO epidemiological alerts, and WHO disease outbreak news provide independent validation against CDC-reported figures.

Structured open-data portals (HealthData.gov, CDC open data API, Our World in Data, Project Tycho) may provide machine-readable Measles case or death counts for the US in 2025, enabling cross-validation against extracted narrative records.

Peer-reviewed outbreak investigations, epidemiological studies, and MMWR reports (treated as literature) may contain granular case counts, hospitalization rates, demographic breakdowns, and case definitions for Measles in the US in 2025.

Reputable news outlets (Reuters, AP, NPR, ProMED-mail, CIDRAP) and situation reports may surface early outbreak signals, state-level case counts, or death reports during Q1 2025 that precede official agency publication, guiding targeted official source retrieval.

iterative_source_discovery_summary.final_coverage_assessment:
Coverage is strong across all primary target fields:

1. NATIONAL CASE COUNT (Q1 2025): The MMWR report (mm7414a1, cdc.gov) provides 800 total cases through April 17, 2025, with 82% concentrated in NM/OK/TX. The second MMWR (mm7520a1, cdc.gov) isolates 325 confirmed cases in West Texas specifically for January 20–March 18, 2025 — directly within the Q1 window. The MMWR (mm7523a2, cdc.gov) covers January 29–February 28, 2025 with 207 confirmed Texas cases.

2. DEATHS: Three deaths confirmed nationally (mm7414a1); one death in West Texas during Jan 20–Mar 18 (mm7520a1); Wikipedia snippet corroborates three deaths (two children in Lubbock, one adult in Lea County, NM) — consistent with MMWR figures.

3. HOSPITALIZATIONS: 60 hospitalized in West Texas Jan 20–Mar 18 (mm7520a1, CIDRAP corroboration); 85 total nationally through April 17 (mm7414a1).

4. SUBNATIONAL LOCATIONS: Texas (Gaines County, South Plains/West Texas, Lubbock, Harris/Houston, Rockwall, Travis), New Mexico (Lea County), Oklahoma (linked cases March 11, 2025), Maryland (Howard County) — all documented in accepted candidates.

5. DATES: Outbreak onset January 20–29, 2025; February 28 interim count; March 11 Oklahoma linkage; March 18 Q1 endpoint — all within the 2025-01-01 to 2025-03-31 window.

6. INTERNATIONAL CROSS-VALIDATION: PAHO situation reports (paho.org) surfaced in iteration 2, confirming 2025 US measles activity in the Americas context. PAHO Situation Report #1 (EW 1–12, 2026) references 2025 full-year US data (2,288 cases); these are post-Q1 but provide retrospective validation.

7. SOURCE DIVERSITY: CDC.gov (4 results, including 2 MMWR reports directly covering Q1), CIDRAP (2 results corroborating MMWR), PAHO.org (4 results for international validation), MSK library guide (secondary aggregator with county-level detail), Wikipedia (contextual corroboration), news/clinical outlets (surepoint-er, respiratory-therapy.com for outbreak timeline).

REMAINING MINOR GAPS: (a) No direct DSHS Texas primary press release URL was surfaced (site: operator queries did not return dshs.texas.gov results directly); (b) No NMDOH (nmhealth.org) primary source appeared; (c) No Oklahoma OSDH primary press release. However, these state-level primary sources are referenced within the MMWR reports and MSK guide, and the MMWR data is authoritative enough to satisfy the collection task without requiring the underlying state press releases as separate candidates.
iterative_source_discovery_summary.final_trustworthiness_assessment: High. The dominant sources are CDC MMWR peer-reviewed surveillance reports (cdc.gov, two directly Q1-relevant reports), CIDRAP (University of Minnesota, citing MMWR), and PAHO (international organization). The MMWR reports carry the highest epidemiological authority for US surveillance data. CIDRAP independently corroborates the MMWR figures. PAHO provides international cross-validation. Secondary sources (Wikipedia, MSK guide, news outlets) are consistent with MMWR figures and add subnational detail. No contradictions between authoritative sources were detected. The surepoint-er.com and respiratory-therapy.com results cite DSHS figures but cover the full outbreak (through August 2025) — they must be used carefully to extract only Q1-relevant data points.

source_discovery_summary.stop_reason: Maximum iteration limit reached (2/2). Evidence coverage is sufficient: national case counts, subnational (state/county) breakdowns, deaths, hospitalizations, and international cross-validation are all represented in the accepted candidate set. No critical unresolvable gaps remain within the Q1 2025 window.

This source is hosted on pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PubMed Central), a highly authoritative and reputable repository operated by the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI/NLM). The domain and publisher carry strong institutional authority (authority_score=0.95). The title — "Measles resurgence in the United States: epidemiological and ..." — is directly relevant to the target disease (Measles) and geography (United States), and the query alignment is strong.

However, several factors constrain the overall credibility and role assignment for this specific collection task:

1. **Source type mismatch**: The source is tagged as `news_and_situation_report`, but PMC articles are peer-reviewed or preprint literature. This mismatch between the assigned source_type and the actual nature of a PMC-hosted article is a meaningful metadata inconsistency that warrants attention. PMC articles should typically be classified as `peer_reviewed_literature`, which ranks higher in the collection spec's source_priority hierarchy.

2. **Role assignment as "context"**: The deterministic layer assigned this source to a `context` role rather than `primary_collection`. For a public health case and outbreak collection task, PMC literature — even if highly relevant — is generally secondary to official public health agency reports (e.g., CDC, state health departments). The context role is appropriate unless the article contains primary surveillance data not available elsewhere.

3. **Screening/critic disagreement flag**: The `screening_and_critic_disagree` risk flag is present, indicating internal pipeline tension about this source's role or credibility classification. This is a meaningful signal that the source's classification may not be stable and merits human review.

4. **Data granularity is moderate** (data_granularity_score=0.68): The source may not provide the structured, field-level data (confirmed cases, hospitalizations, deaths by date and subnational location) required by the collection spec. PMC articles often present aggregated or analyzed data rather than raw surveillance counts.

5. **Timeliness is moderate** (timeliness_score=0.72): For a Q1 2025 time window (January–March 2025), a PMC article with PMC ID PMC12825560 — a very high PMC ID suggesting very recent publication — may reflect data that is current but not yet fully peer-reviewed or finalized. The article's publication lag relative to the outbreak period is unknown without retrieval.

6. **No snippet available**: The absence of a snippet means no direct evidence of extractable data fields (cases_confirmed, deaths, hospitalizations, subnational_location, date_reported) can be confirmed from metadata alone.

7. **Source type misclassification risk**: If this is actually a peer-reviewed article, it should be re-classified as `peer_reviewed_literature` in the pipeline, which would elevate its priority rank in the source_preferences hierarchy (rank 4 vs. rank 5 for news_and_situation_report).

**Overall advisory**: Retain as a `context` source unless human review confirms it contains primary surveillance data tables with required fields. Flag for source_type reclassification review. Do not use as a substitute for CDC or state health department primary sources.

This source is published on publications.aap.org, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) publications platform — a highly respected professional medical organization. However, the specific article is categorized as "AAP News," which is a news/journalism product rather than a peer-reviewed journal article or official surveillance report. This distinction is critical: AAP News articles typically summarize or report on data from primary sources (e.g., CDC, state health departments) rather than originating primary surveillance data themselves. As a result, the authority score (0.48) and independence score (0.42) are appropriately penalized. The deterministic credibility score of 0.50 is reasonable but may slightly undervalue the institutional prestige of the AAP domain. The source is best treated as a high-quality secondary/contextual source that may cite or reference primary CDC or state-level data — making it useful for corroboration and context, but not for direct case count extraction without tracing back to the cited primary source. The "screening_and_critic_disagree" flag warrants attention: if a screening pass rated this higher than the critic pass, the discrepancy likely stems from the AAP domain's strong institutional signal being offset by the news-article format and secondary nature of the content. The missing publisher field is a minor metadata gap, likely resolvable by confirming AAP as publisher. The role assignment of "context" is appropriate and well-supported.

This source presents several compounding credibility concerns that warrant careful advisory review, even though the deterministic assessment did not flag it for human review.

**1. URL Date Mismatch (Critical Flag):** The canonical URL contains `/2026/04/09/` — a 2026 publication date — while the collection task targets Q1 2025 (January–March 2025). This is a significant temporal mismatch. A 2026-dated article reporting on a 2025 outbreak may be retrospective, but it may also contain updated or revised figures that do not reflect the state of knowledge during the target window. This distinction is critical for accurate time-windowed data collection and is not captured in the deterministic risk flags.

**2. Publisher Unknown:** The `publisher` field is null. While the domain `healthbeat.org` is identifiable, the absence of a named publisher organization reduces accountability and makes editorial independence difficult to assess. This compounds the `independence_unclear` and `missing_publisher` flags already raised deterministically.

**3. Source Type and Priority Tier:** As a `news_and_situation_report`, this source sits at the lowest tier of the collection spec's `source_priority` hierarchy. It should only be used when higher-priority sources (official public health agencies, structured databases, peer-reviewed literature) are unavailable or insufficient for a given data point.

**4. Role Assignment — 'Context' is Appropriate but Requires Discipline:** The deterministic assessment correctly assigns this source the role of `context`. However, given the URL date anomaly, even contextual use should be flagged: any figures cited from this article must be cross-referenced against official CDC or state health department sources before being recorded as evidence.

**5. Screening and Critic Disagreement:** The `screening_and_critic_disagree` risk flag is present but unexplained. This is a meaningful signal that internal pipeline components reached different conclusions about this source, and the basis for that disagreement is not documented. This alone warrants a closer look.

**6. Underreporting Framing:** The article title explicitly states "experts warn cases are going unreported." While this is a legitimate public health concern, it also signals that the article may present speculative or estimated figures rather than confirmed surveillance counts — a known extraction risk for measles data, as noted in the disease intelligence summary.

**7. No Snippet Available:** With `snippet: null`, there is no metadata-level preview of the article's actual content, data claims, or sourcing. Any extraction from this article would require full content review, which is not possible in this advisory context.

**Summary:** The deterministic score of 0.484 (low credibility) and role of `context` are appropriate. However, the 2026 URL date relative to a 2025 target window is a material concern not surfaced in the deterministic flags, and the `screening_and_critic_disagree` flag is unresolved. Human review is advisable before this source is used even in a contextual capacity.

This source is a PDF situation report published on the Yale Health / Yale School of Public Health (YSPH) domain, titled "MEASLES – THE AMERICAS 2025–2026," dated February 15, 2026 (file path: 2026-02). Several factors inform this advisory assessment:

1. **Institutional affiliation is credible but not authoritative for primary surveillance data.** Yale School of Public Health is a respected academic institution, but yalehealth.yale.edu is a university health services portal, not a primary public health surveillance agency (e.g., CDC, PAHO, state health departments). The YSPH VMOC (Viral and Molecular Outbreak Consortium or similar) is an academic monitoring unit — its reports synthesize and contextualize data rather than originate it. This limits its role to secondary/contextual use.

2. **Temporal mismatch is a significant concern.** The file path contains "2026-02," indicating a February 2026 publication date. The collection window is Q1 2025 (January–March 2025). While the report covers "2025–2026" and may contain retrospective Q1 2025 data, any figures presented will be retrospective summaries, not contemporaneous surveillance records. Cumulative vs. incident count confusion risk is elevated.

3. **Geographic scope is broader than required.** The title specifies "THE AMERICAS," not the United States specifically. Geographic granularity for US-only, subnational, or state-level data extraction is likely limited. Sub-national fields (subnational_location, locality) may be sparsely populated or absent.

4. **PDF format reduces machine readability.** Structured field extraction (cases_confirmed, hospitalizations, deaths, etc.) will require manual parsing. Evidence quotes must be carefully attributed to avoid conflating regional aggregates with US-specific figures.

5. **Publisher field is null.** While the domain implies YSPH authorship, the absence of an explicit publisher declaration is a provenance gap that warrants caution, particularly for a report that may be cited in downstream records.

6. **Independence is unclear.** The report likely synthesizes CDC, PAHO, and state health department data without independent data collection. Any figures extracted should be traced back to their primary source before being ingested as collection records.

7. **Screening and critic disagree flag** is present in the deterministic assessment, indicating internal scoring tension that warrants human advisory review despite the deterministic system not flagging it for human review. The LLM advisory layer recommends elevating this for a brief human check given the temporal mismatch and geographic scope concerns.

In 2025, 14,503 measles cases were reported, including 32 deaths. This follows a marked rise in cases during 2025, with continued acceleration observed in early 2026.  Genotyping information indicate that the D8 lineage has been identified across multiple countries and is associated with outbreaks in at least ten countries, suggesting widespread circulation of this strain in the Region.  The highest number of cases in 2026 have been reported in Mexico (n= 8,315), Guatemala (n= 3,687), the United States of America (n= 1,664), and Canada (n= 733), with ongoing transmission documented in Bolivia and other countries across the Region.  All age groups are affected; however, the highest number of cases has been reported among children, particularly those aged 1–9 years, followed by children and adolescents aged 10–19 years. Incidence rates are highest among children under one year of age.  A substantial proportion of cases occur among unvaccinated individuals, with available data indicating that approximately two-thirds of confirmed cases have no documented history of measles vaccination. |

metric_row_extraction_audit.heading_context: ## Preliminary Conclusions and Actions
metric_row_extraction_audit.row_quote: Decreases in measles vaccination coverage worldwide have increased the risk for larger measles outbreaks, especially in undervaccinated communities ([About Measles | CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/about/index.html#cdc_disease_basics_population-who-is-at-risk)). On August 18, 2025, the [Texas measles outbreak was declared over](https://www.dshs.texas.gov/news-alerts/texas-announces-end-west-texas-measles-outbreak), having comprised 762 confirmed cases, 99 hospitalizations, and a second measles-associated death. Although the source of this outbreak remains unknown, internationally imported cases have been associated with outbreaks among other close-knit U.S. communities with low vaccination coverage (*3*,*4*).
